capabilities.action: Read signed coordinates on an axis and subtract two coordinate values, keeping the sign.
capabilities.success_criterion: State which direction a negative or positive result names, without dropping the sign. Draft explanation only (not Mathematics-provider-accepted): on a signed number line, going from a point at coordinate b to a point at coordinate a is the displacement a-b; the sign of the result names the direction, its size names the distance. This is the one-axis case that a vector component uses along each axis independently.

capabilities.action: Obtain the hypotenuse length from two perpendicular leg lengths.
capabilities.success_criterion: Apply length_of_hypotenuse = sqrt(leg1^2 + leg2^2) with nonnegative lengths, independent of either leg's sign. Draft explanation only (not Mathematics-provider-accepted): two perpendicular signed components are two legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the vector's magnitude. Squaring removes the sign, so the same magnitude formula applies regardless of which quadrant the vector points into; the signs are only needed back again for direction.

capabilities.action: Use sine and cosine ratios in a right triangle to obtain perpendicular leg magnitudes from a hypotenuse magnitude and an acute reference angle.
capabilities.success_criterion: Given hypotenuse V and acute angle theta measured from one perpendicular axis, calculate adjacent magnitude V cos(theta) and opposite magnitude V sin(theta), then leave physical signs to the declared vector-axis convention. Draft bridge explanation only; Mathematics-provider acceptance remains required.

capabilities.success_criterion: Given two directed quantities, state whether equal magnitude is sufficient to identify the same vector and name direction as additional information.

microtopics.title: Vector information versus magnitude-only information
microtopics.badge_reason: The words are simple, but learners often treat equal length or equal speed as if it fully identifies a directed quantity.
entry_assumptions: Can compare ordinary nonnegative sizes and recognise that an arrow has an orientation.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Equal magnitude alone does not determine a vector because direction is part of the quantity.

teaching_path.action: Place two equal-length arrows from the same start, one pointing east and one west.
teaching_path.why_valid: Holding the drawn length fixed isolates direction as the only changed feature.
teaching_path.output: Two arrows with the same magnitude and opposite directions.

teaching_path.action: State the magnitude of each arrow, then state the direction of each arrow separately.
teaching_path.why_valid: Magnitude answers only how large; the direction statement carries information the shared magnitude does not.
teaching_path.output: Both magnitudes are equal, but the vectors are different because their directions differ.

teaching_path.action: Reverse one arrow without changing its length and check which description changes.
teaching_path.why_valid: A pure reversal preserves magnitude while changing the vector, directly testing whether magnitude alone identifies the directed quantity.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Two directed quantities with the same magnitude are the same vector.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two arrows are both 5 units long, one east and one west. Are they the same vector?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the length fixed and compare direction. Equal magnitude does not make two oppositely directed quantities the same vector.

exit_task.prompt: Two arrows have equal length. One points north and the other south. State what is the same, what is different, and whether they are the same vector.

answer.summary: They have the same magnitude but opposite directions, so they are not the same vector.
reasoning: The equal arrow lengths represent equal magnitude.
North and south are different directions.
A vector is identified by magnitude together with direction, so equal magnitude alone is insufficient.
answer.check: Reverse the south-pointing arrow without changing its length; it can then match the north-pointing vector.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The task checks the vector-versus-magnitude distinction without requiring component arithmetic.

microtopics.research_contribution: The vector-versus-magnitude distinction is standard; this equal-length opposite-arrow teaching sequence is author-created and pending independent scientific/pedagogical review.

predict.prompt: Two arrows have equal length but point in opposite directions. Before reading on, are they the same vector?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Equal length gives equal magnitude, but opposite directions make the vectors different.

attempt.produces: A one-sentence comparison naming what is shared and what differs.

rubric.criterion: Names equal magnitude as the shared property.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating size from full vector identity.

rubric.criterion: Names opposite direction as the difference.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating direction as part of the vector.

accepted: Same magnitude, opposite direction, therefore different vectors.
rejected: They are the same because both arrows have the same length.

route.ask: What did we hold fixed when the two arrow lengths were made equal?
route.why_this_ask: It isolates magnitude as the shared quantity.

route.ask: What changed when one arrow was reversed?
route.why_this_ask: It makes direction the single distinguishing feature.

route.ask: If the magnitude stayed fixed while the vector changed, what extra information must a vector contain?
route.why_this_ask: The learner states the distinction rather than receiving it as a definition.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path states the two descriptions explicitly; reconstruction starts from the reversal test and asks the learner to infer what magnitude omits.

boundary_test.prompt: If two arrows have equal length and also point in the same direction, what else would have to differ for them not to represent the same free vector?
boundary_test.answer: Nothing about the free vector itself; with the same magnitude and direction they represent the same free vector even if drawn in different places.
boundary_test.confirms: Magnitude plus direction identifies the free vector; drawing location is not another vector property.

microtopics.title: Choosing axes and keeping components signed
microtopics.badge_reason: Axis choice is conventional, but once the positive directions are declared the component signs are fixed and cannot be chosen for convenience.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish vector information from magnitude-only information.
Signed coordinate reading on one axis is available or bridged.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The physical vector stays fixed when axes are redeclared; only the signed numerical description changes according to the declared positive directions.

teaching_path.action: Declare positive directions for both axes before reading any component.
teaching_path.why_valid: A component sign has meaning only relative to a stated positive axis direction.
teaching_path.output: For example: east is +x and north is +y.

teaching_path.action: Read the component along each axis with the sign fixed by whether the arrow points with or against that positive direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: The sign records orientation along the declared axis; it is not an after-the-fact label.
teaching_path.output: A westward horizontal component is negative when east is declared positive.

teaching_path.action: Reverse one declared positive axis while keeping the physical arrow unchanged and update only the component on that axis.
teaching_path.why_valid: Changing the coordinate convention changes the signed description, not the physical vector.
teaching_path.output: Exactly one component sign flips when exactly one positive axis is reversed.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A component should be made positive because the object is moving 'forward'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If east is declared positive and the vector points west, is the x-component positive or negative?
misconceptions.repair: Use only the declared positive axis. A component pointing against it is negative regardless of the story's word 'forward'.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Changing the axis convention changes the physical vector.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If the positive x-direction is reversed while the arrow stays fixed, did the arrow itself reverse?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the arrow fixed and change only the signed coordinate description. The convention changes; the physical vector does not.

exit_task.prompt: Under east-positive and north-positive axes a vector is (5,-2). The x-axis stays the same, but south is now declared positive. State the new signed components and explain which sign changed.

answer.summary: The new components are (5,2). Only the vertical sign changes because only the vertical positive direction was reversed.
reasoning: The east-positive x-axis is unchanged, so the x-component remains +5.
South is now positive instead of north, so the same downward component is +2 rather than -2.
The physical vector was not changed; only its coordinate description was.
answer.check: Restore north-positive and the vertical component returns to -2.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The numbers are declared in the prompt; the task checks sign transformation under an axis reversal rather than a derived magnitude.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created axis-convention drill; independent scientific/pedagogical review pending.

predict.prompt: A fixed arrow has components (5,-2) when north is positive. If only the vertical positive direction is reversed, which component sign should change?
predict.defensible_answer: Only the vertical component changes sign; the horizontal convention did not change.

attempt.produces: The transformed ordered pair plus one sentence tying each sign to the declared positive axes.

rubric.evidence_of: Tracking only the axis convention that changed.
Reading sign from the newly declared vertical positive direction.

accepted: (5,2), because east-positive stayed fixed and south-positive reverses the vertical sign.
rejected: (-5,2), which flips both components even though only one axis convention changed.

route.ask: Which physical arrow did we change?
route.why_this_ask: The correct answer is none; this separates coordinate convention from physical motion.
It isolates the single coordinate rule that can affect the ordered pair.

route.ask: Which component lies on that axis, and what sign must it now have?
route.why_this_ask: The learner performs the sign transformation from the declaration.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path demonstrates the sign rule. Reconstruction begins by holding the physical arrow fixed and lets the learner identify the one convention change that can alter the representation.

boundary_test.prompt: If both positive axis directions are reversed while the physical arrow stays fixed, what happens to the ordered pair?
boundary_test.confirms: Component signs belong to the declared coordinate convention, not to an intrinsic positive/negative label on the vector.

microtopics.title: Subtraction as addition of the reversed vector
microtopics.badge_reason: The reverse-then-add construction is a genuine model shift from ordinary addition, even though the component arithmetic looks similar.
entry_assumptions: Can read signed components under declared axes.
Can distinguish vector direction from magnitude.
microtopics.inferential_jump: See P - Q as P + (-Q): reverse Q's arrowhead without changing its length, then apply tail-to-head addition.

teaching_path.why_valid: Negating a vector keeps its length and flips both signed components.
teaching_path.output: -Q has the same magnitude as Q and the opposite direction.

teaching_path.action: Translate -Q to the head of P without rotating it.
teaching_path.why_valid: A free vector's meaning depends only on length and direction, not on where it is drawn.

teaching_path.action: Draw the resultant from the tail of P to the head of the translated -Q.
teaching_path.why_valid: Tail-to-head addition gives the vector sum, here P + (-Q) = P - Q.

teaching_path.action: Reconcile the drawn resultant with component-wise signed subtraction.
teaching_path.why_valid: The graphical construction and component subtraction are two representations of the same vector operation and must agree.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Vector subtraction means drawing both vectors from the same origin and connecting their two tips in whichever order looks right.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Which endpoint does the subtraction arrow start from: the tip of P or the tip of Q?
misconceptions.repair: Perform the explicit reverse-then-add construction (GS-1 to GS-3); the two-tips shortcut hides the observer order and is easy to reverse by mistake.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Reversing a vector changes its magnitude.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If an arrow is flipped end for end without changing its drawn length, did its magnitude change?
misconceptions.repair: Reverse only the direction. Keep the arrow length fixed; vector negation changes orientation, not magnitude.

exit_task.prompt: In one declared x-y frame, P=(6,0) and Q=(0,8). Construct P-Q as P+(-Q) and state the resultant signed components. Explain one check that confirms the subtraction order.

answer.summary: P-Q=(6,-8). Reverse Q to (0,-8), add it tail-to-head to P, and verify that direct component subtraction gives the same ordered pair.
reasoning: Negating Q reverses its direction without changing its length, giving -Q=(0,-8).
Tail-to-head addition of P and -Q produces a resultant with components (6,-8).
Direct subtraction gives (6-0,0-8)=(6,-8), confirming the construction and order.
answer.check: Swapping the order gives Q-P=(-6,8), the exact negative of P-Q.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit task checks construction, component subtraction, and operand-order reversal; it does not require a magnitude calculation.

microtopics.research_contribution: NCERT motivates the graphical construction; PhET is a candidate exploration route, not executed evidence. The reverse-then-add teaching sequence itself is author-created pending scientific/pedagogical review. These exact component values (6,0) and (0,8) recur with physical meaning as A and B's velocities in MIC-COMMON-INTERVAL/MIC-GEOMETRIC-CHECK (BUCKET-RELATIVE-MOTION): this is a deliberate shared anchor rehearsing the same arithmetic before it carries physical meaning, not accidental duplication.

predict.prompt: Before drawing, if P-Q is rewritten as P+(-Q), what must happen to Q?
predict.defensible_answer: Q must be reversed without changing its length.

attempt.produces: A reverse-then-add arrow construction plus the resultant signed components.

rubric.criterion: Q is reversed before tail-to-head addition.
rubric.evidence_of: Using subtraction as addition of the additive inverse.

rubric.criterion: The graphical resultant and signed-component subtraction agree.
rubric.evidence_of: Reconciling two representations of the same operation.

accepted: Reverse Q, place -Q at the head of P, draw the resultant, and obtain the same ordered pair by subtracting components.
rejected: Connect the two arrow tips without fixing operand order; this can silently produce Q-P instead of P-Q.

route.ask: Which vector is being subtracted, and what is its additive inverse?
route.why_this_ask: It restores operand order before any drawing.

route.ask: Where should the tail of the reversed vector be placed?
route.why_this_ask: It reconstructs the tail-to-head sum rather than a memorized tip-to-tip shortcut.

route.ask: What signed components should the same result have?
route.why_this_ask: The second representation provides an independent order check.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path demonstrates reverse-then-add. Reconstruction withholds the construction and asks the learner to rebuild it from operand order, then check it component-wise.

boundary_test.prompt: If P and Q are identical vectors, what does P-Q produce?
boundary_test.confirms: Subtracting a vector from itself cancels both signed components and leaves no direction to preserve.

microtopics.title: When the simple v_A/B = v_A - v_B relation needs frame qualification (research-boundary note)
microtopics.badge_reason: Not a Grade 9 assessment badge: this is a RESEARCH-depth boundary note, included only to show where the taught relation stops applying.
entry_assumptions: Has completed MIC-GEOMETRIC-CHECK and accepts v_A/B = v_A - v_B for translating, nonrotating frames.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Recognise that the simple subtraction relation assumes both frames are nonrotating and non-relativistic; naming when it needs qualification is itself the (bounded) research task, not deriving the replacement mathematics.

teaching_path.action: Restate the two conditions already attached to REL-RELATIVE-VELOCITY: parallel nonrotating axes, classical (non-relativistic) speeds.
teaching_path.why_valid: Those conditions were declared, not incidental, when the relation was derived.
teaching_path.output: The relation is conditional, not universal.

teaching_path.action: Name, without deriving, the two regimes where each condition can fail: a rotating reference frame (needs Coriolis/centrifugal terms) and speeds approaching light speed (needs relativistic velocity addition).
teaching_path.why_valid: Naming the failure regime is a defensible research-boundary claim; deriving the replacement transformation is graduate-level and explicitly out of scope here.
teaching_path.output: Two named boundaries, no new formula taught.

teaching_path.action: State that this note is excluded from Grade 9 assessment claims and is not required for MIC-GEOMETRIC-CHECK's exit task.
teaching_path.why_valid: Research-depth material is segregated from exam scope (TOPIC_WORKFLOW.md); a badge cannot be raised to smuggle in graduate prerequisites.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Since the school formula is 'wrong' in general, it should not be taught or trusted at all.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Does a merry-go-round or a near-light-speed spacecraft appear anywhere in the Grade 9 assessment scope?
misconceptions.repair: A model's stated domain of validity is what makes it correct within that domain; the Grade 9 translating-frame case is exactly where the taught relation applies.

exit_task.prompt: Name (without deriving) one situation where v_A/B = v_A - v_B would need an additional term, and state whether that situation is in the Grade 9 assessment scope.

answer.summary: A rotating reference frame (e.g. observations made from a spinning platform) needs an additional Coriolis-type term; this is outside the Grade 9 assessment scope.
reasoning: The derivation in MIC-COMMON-INTERVAL assumed parallel, nonrotating axes at every instant.
A rotating frame violates that assumption, so the simple difference no longer accounts for the frame's own rotation.
answer.check: The excluded-topics list for this run already names 'Rotating frames and Coriolis terms' as out of scope, consistent with this boundary note.
acceptable_alternatives: Relativistic velocity addition, for speeds approaching c, is also acceptable.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: This microtopic states where the relation stops applying; its exit answer names two boundary conditions and asserts no computed value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Implements the run's configured stress extension (stress.one_extension: 'a separate research-oriented model-boundary bucket on when simple relative-velocity subtraction needs frame qualifications'). Deliberately does not teach rotating-frame or relativistic mathematics; names the boundary only, per TOPIC_WORKFLOW.md's Research-depth Gravity precedent (a conceptual bridge may be authored while derivation-level release stays blocked).

relations.meaning: Subtracting a vector means adding its reverse; component-wise this is (P-Q)_x = P_x - Q_x and (P-Q)_y = P_y - Q_y.

symbols.meaning: First vector in a named common frame
Second vector in the same frame
Q reversed: same magnitude, opposite direction

conditions: P and Q are expressed along the same declared axes.
Reversal preserves magnitude and negates every component.
Free vectors may be translated without rotation for the graphical construction.

derivation.action: Define -Q as the vector with Q's magnitude and the opposite direction.
derivation.why_valid: This is the definition of vector negation.
Subtraction is defined as addition of the additive inverse, exactly as for signed numbers.

limits: This is a general definition of vector subtraction; REL-RELATIVE-VELOCITY is its specialisation to two objects' velocities in a common frame.
checks: P - P = 0 for any vector P.
Reversing the order negates the result: Q - P = -(P - Q).

representations.purpose: Show a single vector's signed components against declared axes and its nonnegative magnitude.
required_elements: Labelled vector with tail at the origin and arrowhead at the endpoint
Signed component readout along each axis
read_order: Compute the nonnegative magnitude via the right-triangle bridge.
instance_constraints: One length scale for both axes.
A zero vector has no assigned direction.
accessibility: Use labels and line styles as well as colour.
misleading_alternatives: An arrow drawn without labelled axes.
Correct magnitude paired with an unlabelled or ambiguous direction.

scene.frame: One common east/north frame, equal scale on both axes.
scene.caption: w = (3, 4) m/s: the arrow's position is fixed by its two signed components, and its length is a consequence of them rather than a third independent number.

correspondence.element: Labelled vector with tail at the origin and arrowhead at the endpoint
correspondence.in_words: the arrow itself, whose length is the magnitude and whose slant is the direction

representations.purpose: Show why subtracting Q means adding the reversed -Q, tail-to-head, distinct from the direct component-subtraction shortcut.
required_elements: Resultant labelled P-Q, with tail/head and scale
read_order: Reverse Q without changing its length.
Place the reversed vector at the head of P without rotating it.
Draw the resultant and compare its components with direct subtraction.
instance_constraints: One length scale for both axes and all instance vectors.
A zero resultant has no assigned direction.
accessibility: Use labels and line styles as well as colour.
Inspect arrowheads and text at final size.
misleading_alternatives: Two unrelated arrows with no subtraction construction.
Correct magnitude with the wrong observer/subtraction order.

scene.frame: One common east/north frame, at one length scale for every vector drawn.
scene.caption: P - Q is built by reversing Q and placing it at the head of P. The resultant (6, -8) m/s is longer than either vector, which a component-subtraction shortcut gives without ever showing why.

correspondence.in_words: the vector being subtracted from, drawn from the frame's origin
the vector being taken away, before it is turned around
the same arrow pointing the other way, the same length as before

question_families.title: Distinguish, represent or subtract vectors
solution_structure: Read or subtract signed components in the declared order.
Apply the right-triangle bridge only if a magnitude is requested.
State direction from the signed components, not the magnitude.

questions.stem: Two directed arrows have the same length but point in opposite directions. Can the shared magnitude alone make them the same vector? Explain what information signed components preserve that magnitude does not.

answer.summary: No. Equal magnitude does not make opposite arrows the same vector; signed components preserve direction relative to declared axes while magnitude keeps only nonnegative size.
reasoning: Magnitude records size and is nonnegative.
Opposite arrows can therefore share the same magnitude.
Their signed components change sign and preserve the directional information that distinguishes the two vectors.
answer.check: Reverse every component sign of one nonzero vector. Its magnitude stays the same while its direction reverses.

hints.text: Separate the question 'how large?' from the question 'which way?'
Ask what happens to component signs when a vector is reversed.

difficulty.basis: Explains why vector equality requires both equal magnitude and identical direction, and how signed components encode directional orientation.

conventions.statement: Components are read against declared directions: x counts east and y counts north. Nothing in this bucket has a component until those directions are stated.
A magnitude is written without a sign and a component is written with one. Both describe the same vector, and swapping them is the error this bucket exists to prevent.
